introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
How justified were German criticisms of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 between Germany and the Allied and Associated Powers, and came into force in January 1920. Germans condemned it from the beginning as a *Diktat* (dictated peace): they had not been allowed to negotiate and had to sign under threat of renewed war. Their main criticisms concerned the war guilt clause, reparations, territorial losses, disarmament and the exclusion of Germany from the League of Nations. The question is how far these criticisms were justified. It is argued that some were justified, especially on the manner of the settlement and some territorial decisions, but that others were exaggerated, since the treaty was not as harsh as the German peace imposed on others and left Germany a united and potentially strong state.

**1. Criticisms that were largely justified.**
- *A dictated peace and broken expectations.* Germans had accepted the armistice of November 1918 expecting a peace based on President Wilson's Fourteen Points, and the treaty was drawn up by the victors without German delegates and could only be accepted or refused.
- *The "war guilt" clause (Article 231).* It stated that Germany and her allies accepted responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war. It was intended as a legal basis for reparations, but Germans felt it as a national humiliation, and many historians agree that responsibility for the war was shared.
- *Territorial decisions and self-determination.* The treaty took Alsace-Lorraine (returned to France), Eupen-Malmedy (to Belgium), North Schleswig (to Denmark after a plebiscite), the Polish Corridor and most of Posen and West Prussia (to Poland), and made Danzig a free city; the Saar was placed under League of Nations administration for fifteen years, with its coal mines given to France, and Germany lost all colonies as League mandates. Some of these decisions placed millions of Germans under foreign rule, while Germans in Austria and the Sudetenland were forbidden to unite with Germany, which contradicted the principle of self-determination that the Allies claimed to support.
- *Disarmament that was one-sided.* The army was limited to 100,000 men without conscription, tanks or an air force, the navy was limited, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by Allied forces for up to fifteen years. Germany was disarmed while the Allies did not disarm, even though Wilson had promised a general reduction of armaments.
- *Reparations.* In 1921 the total was fixed at 132 billion gold marks, which many economists, such as John Maynard Keynes in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace* (1919), considered more than Germany could pay, and the loss of the coal and iron regions and colonies reduced her ability to pay.

**2. Criticisms that were exaggerated or not justified.**
- *Germany had imposed harsher terms.* In the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) Germany took huge territory and resources from Russia, and in 1871 she had imposed an indemnity and annexed Alsace-Lorraine, so the complaint of a harsh peace was not consistent with her own conduct.
- *Germany was not destroyed.* She was not divided or occupied, and kept most of her territory, her industries and her population, which was larger than that of France. Several of the territorial losses were returns of lands that were not German by population (Posen and the Corridor had large Polish populations, and Alsace-Lorraine had been French until 1871). Many plebiscites were held (North Schleswig, parts of East Prussia, Upper Silesia in 1921).
- *The Allies had a case for security and compensation.* France had been invaded twice in fifty years, and its northern industrial districts had been destroyed in the war, so the demands for reparations and guarantees were understandable. The treaty was a compromise between Wilson's ideals, Clemenceau's wish for security and Lloyd George's moderation, and was less harsh than French demands (France had asked for the Rhineland to be separated).
- *The criticism was politically used.* The war-guilt and "stab in the back" myths allowed German governments and later the Nazis to blame the treaty for economic and political problems that were partly caused by the war itself, by inflation and by German policy, and later reparations were reduced (Dawes Plan 1924, Young Plan 1929) and most were never paid.

**Conclusion.** German criticism was justified to a considerable extent regarding the way the treaty was imposed, the war-guilt clause, the failure to apply self-determination consistently and the one-sided disarmament. However, the claim that the treaty was a crushing and unprecedented punishment was exaggerated: Germany kept her unity and economic base and the terms were no harsher than those she had imposed on others. The treaty was therefore neither as fair as the Allies claimed nor as unjust as Germans said.
